name: Cervical cancer & HPV
sources: International Agency for Research on Cancer

what_is_it.heading: Cervical cancer in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Cervical cancer is cancer of the cervix — the lower part of the womb. Almost all cases (over 99%) are caused by long-term infection with high-risk types of HPV (Human Papillomavirus).
paragraphs: HPV is extremely common — most sexually active people catch it at some point. The body clears most HPV infections within a year or two. But if a high-risk type persists for 10–15 years, it can cause cells in the cervix to change slowly into pre-cancer, then cancer.

This long timeline is what makes cervical cancer one of the most preventable cancers in the world. Screening (Pap smear or HPV test) catches cell changes years before cancer develops — when treatment is simple. The HPV vaccine prevents the infections that cause it in the first place.

items.headline: Second most common
items.body: Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer in SA women. The highest rates are in women aged 35 to 55.

items.headline: 99% HPV
items.body: Over 99% of cervical cancers are caused by long-term HPV infection. Stopping HPV stops the cancer.

items.headline: Free vaccine
items.body: The HPV vaccine is free for Grade 5 girls (and now boys in many provinces) through the school programme. Best given before sexual debut.

items.headline: Pap smears save lives
items.body: Free Pap smear every 10 years from age 30 at government clinics. Every 3 years if HIV positive. Catches changes before cancer.

pull_quote.text: If every woman in South Africa got vaccinated as a girl and screened in adulthood, we could eliminate cervical cancer within a generation. The tools exist. They are free.

signs.heading: What you might notice
signs.lede: Early cervical changes — including pre-cancer and early cancer — usually cause no symptoms. This is why screening matters. Symptoms appear when cancer is more advanced.

items.title: Early — silent
items.description: Pre-cancer and early cancer usually cause no symptoms. Only a Pap smear or HPV test catches changes this early.

items.title: Later — bleeding
items.description: Bleeding between periods, after sex, or after menopause. Heavier or longer periods than usual. Unusual vaginal discharge.

items.title: Advanced — see a doctor
items.description: Pelvic pain, lower back pain, pain during sex, leg swelling, blood in urine or stool. These need urgent assessment.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.myth: Only women who have many partners get HPV.
items.fact: HPV is extremely common — most sexually active people catch it. Even one partner can transmit it. Vaccination protects regardless of partner history.

items.myth: The HPV vaccine encourages young people to start sex earlier.
items.fact: Years of research show no link between HPV vaccination and earlier sexual activity. The vaccine works best given before any sexual exposure.

items.myth: If I had the HPV vaccine, I do not need Pap smears.
items.fact: The vaccine prevents most but not all high-risk HPV types. Screening is still essential — vaccine plus screening together is the strongest protection.

items.myth: Cervical cancer runs in families — there is nothing I can do.
items.fact: Family history is a small risk factor at most. HPV infection is the cause for almost all cervical cancer — and HPV is preventable and detectable.

prevention.heading: How to protect yourself
prevention.lede: Cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers because there is both a vaccine and effective screening. Every adult woman should know her plan.

items.title: HPV vaccine
items.description: Free in SA for Grade 5 girls (and boys in many provinces). Best before sexual activity starts but works at any age — ask your clinic up to age 45.

items.title: Regular Pap smears
items.description: Free at clinics from age 30, every 10 years if normal. Every 3 years if HIV positive. Start earlier and screen more often if you have a history of abnormal results.

items.title: Condoms
items.description: Reduce HPV transmission but do not eliminate it — HPV can spread from skin not covered by a condom. Still useful, especially with new partners.

items.title: Don't smoke
items.description: Smoking weakens the cervix's ability to clear HPV infection and doubles cervical cancer risk in HPV-positive women.

items.title: If you have a daughter in Grade 5
items.description: Make sure she gets the HPV vaccine through the school programme. Two doses, free, given six months apart. This is the single most powerful cancer-prevention tool we have.

items.title: If you are aged 30 or older
items.description: Book a Pap smear at any government clinic if you have not had one in the last 10 years. Free, takes five minutes, results in 2–4 weeks.

items.title: If you have HIV
items.description: Screening is every 3 years regardless of age, from diagnosis onwards. HPV behaves more aggressively with HIV — do not skip.

items.title: If you have abnormal bleeding
items.description: Bleeding between periods, after sex, or after menopause — see a clinic. Most causes are not cancer, but cervical cancer is one cause that needs catching early.

items.title: If your Pap smear is abnormal
items.description: Do not panic. Most abnormal results are pre-cancer that can be treated in a single visit. Follow up — the system works if you keep your appointments.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: Cervical screening, treatment of pre-cancer, and the HPV vaccine are all free at South African public clinics. The cancer-prevention infrastructure is there — use it.

helplines.name: Find your nearest clinic
helplines.description: Free HPV vaccines, Pap smears, and follow-up of abnormal results
helplines.meta: No appointment · no medical aid required
